slides.title: Sustainable Energy Systems
points: Module 3 explains how chemistry converts, stores and delivers electrical energy.
Nernst equation • concentration cells • batteries • Li-ion • sodium-ion • supercapacitors • SOFC • PV cells • green hydrogen
slides.say: Open by saying modern smart systems need energy that is portable, efficient and sustainable.
slides.ask: Ask students to connect the construction to the direction of ion/electron movement.

slides.title: Module 3 learning path
points: Use the VTU syllabus as the complete checklist.
Explain energy systems and electrochemical energy conversion
Use the Nernst equation and solve concentration-cell numericals
Explain construction and working of concentration cells
Classify batteries and explain Li-ion batteries
Explain sodium-ion batteries for EV applications
Explain asymmetric supercapacitors for IoT and wearable devices
Explain SOFCs, PV cells and green hydrogen production
slides.say: Show students how each topic builds toward sustainable energy devices.

slides.title: Why sustainable energy systems matter
points: Phones, laptops and sensors need high energy density.
Batteries must be powerful, safe and affordable.
Tiny devices need fast, compact energy storage.
Solar cells and green hydrogen reduce fossil-fuel dependence.
slides.say: Ask students where they used stored electrochemical energy today.

slides.title: What is an energy system?
points: Define energy systems in simple engineering language.
An energy system is an arrangement that converts, stores or supplies energy for a useful purpose, often by chemical or electrochemical processes.
slides.say: Tell students Module 3 focuses on electrochemical and sustainable devices.
slides.ask: Ask students to connect the construction to the direction of ion/electron movement.

slides.title: Electrochemical energy conversion
points: Show the core idea behind cells and batteries.
slides.say: Separate electron flow from ion flow.

slides.title: Why the Nernst equation is needed
points: Explain the problem before the formula.
Potential is not fixed when concentration changes.
Practical devices rarely operate at exactly 1 M and 1 atm.
The equation helps decide spontaneity and voltage.
VTU problems often use concentration-cell data.
slides.say: Emphasize that Nernst converts chemical concentration into electrical potential.
slides.ask: Ask students to connect the construction to the direction of ion/electron movement.

slides.title: Nernst equation overview

definition.text: Ecell = E°cell - (RT / nF) ln Q At 298 K: Ecell = E°cell - (0.0591 / n) log Q

points: Exam method: write the equation, define every symbol, substitute values with units, then state what the answer means for the cell.
slides.say: Define Ecell, E°cell, R, T, n, F and Q.
slides.ask: Ask students to connect the construction to the direction of ion/electron movement.

slides.title: Nernst equation for concentration cells

definition.term: Specialize the equation for same-electrode cells.
definition.text: For a concentration cell: E°cell = 0 Ecell = (0.0591 / n) log(Ccathode / Canode) Higher concentration side acts as cathode

points: Exam method: write the equation, define every symbol, substitute values with units, then state what the answer means for the cell.
slides.say: Stress that voltage comes only from concentration difference.

slides.title: What is a concentration cell?
points: A concentration cell has identical electrodes and electrolytes of different concentrations; the concentration difference produces the cell potential.
slides.say: Ask students why E° becomes zero when electrodes are identical.

slides.title: Why concentration cells produce voltage
slides.say: Use the word equalization carefully: it is the thermodynamic tendency.

slides.title: Construction of concentration cell
points: Two identical electrodes are dipped in solutions of the same ion at different concentrations. A salt bridge completes the internal circuit and an external wire allows electron flow.
slides.say: Point to anode, cathode, salt bridge and external wire.
slides.ask: Ask students to connect the construction to the direction of ion/electron movement.

slides.title: Working of a metal-ion concentration cell

slides.title: Cell notation for concentration cell

definition.text: M | Mⁿ⁺(C1) || Mⁿ⁺(C2) | M If C2 > C1: Anode: M | Mⁿ⁺(C1) Cathode: Mⁿ⁺(C2) | M

points: Exam method: write the equation, define every symbol, substitute values with units, then state what the answer means for the cell.
slides.say: Explain left side is conventionally the anode.

slides.title: What is a battery?
points: A battery is an electrochemical device that converts stored chemical energy into electrical energy through redox reactions.
slides.say: Connect the definition to the earlier redox model.
slides.ask: Ask students to connect the construction to the direction of ion/electron movement.

slides.title: Battery classification
points: Classify batteries as per basic chemistry.
Reaction can be reversed by charging
slides.say: Keep this crisp for two-mark questions.
slides.ask: Ask students to connect the construction to the direction of ion/electron movement.

slides.title: Other useful battery categories
points: Activated only when needed; useful for special systems.
Reactants are supplied continuously rather than fully stored inside.
Electrolytes are stored externally and pumped through the cell.
Use solid electrolytes for safety and packaging advantages.
slides.say: Mention these only as overview categories.
slides.ask: Ask students to connect the construction to the direction of ion/electron movement.

slides.title: Why Li-ion batteries dominate devices
points: Stores more energy per unit mass than many older batteries.
Lithium ions shuttle during charge and discharge.
Important for phones, laptops and EVs.
slides.say: Ask students why mobile devices avoid very heavy batteries.
slides.ask: Ask students to connect the construction to the direction of ion/electron movement.

slides.title: Construction of Li-ion battery
points: A typical Li-ion cell contains a graphite anode, lithium metal oxide cathode, organic electrolyte with lithium salt, separator and current collectors.
slides.say: Point at separator as the safety-critical component.
slides.ask: Ask students to connect the construction to the direction of ion/electron movement.

slides.title: Working during discharge
slides.say: State that ions and electrons take different paths.

slides.title: Li-ion battery electrode reactions

definition.text: Discharge idea: Anode: LiC6 → C6 + Li+ + e- Cathode: Li1-xMO2 + xLi+ + xe- → LiMO2 Overall: Li ions shuttle between host materials

points: Exam method: write the equation, define every symbol, substitute values with units, then state what the answer means for the cell.

slides.title: Why sodium-ion batteries are emerging
points: Sodium resources are more widely available than lithium.
Attractive for large-scale storage and affordable EVs.
Na+ ions move between host electrodes.
Useful where cost and resource security matter.
slides.say: Frame sodium-ion as related to Li-ion but not identical.
slides.ask: Ask students to connect the construction to the direction of ion/electron movement.

slides.title: Construction of sodium-ion battery
points: A sodium-ion battery uses a sodium-hosting anode, sodium-containing cathode, separator, electrolyte with sodium salt and current collectors.
slides.say: Explain Na+ is larger than Li+, affecting materials.
slides.ask: Ask students to connect the construction to the direction of ion/electron movement.

slides.say: Ask students to compare with Li-ion working.

slides.title: Sodium-ion battery for EVs
points: May reduce dependence on expensive lithium materials.
Useful where moderate range and affordability matter.
Can support charging infrastructure and grids.
Cell chemistry still needs careful thermal and battery management.
slides.say: Avoid overclaiming; say emerging and application-dependent.

slides.title: What is a supercapacitor?
points: A supercapacitor is an energy-storage device that stores charge at electrode/electrolyte interfaces or through fast surface redox reactions, giving high power density.
slides.say: Contrast with batteries: supercapacitors store energy differently.
slides.ask: Ask students to connect the construction to the direction of ion/electron movement.

slides.title: Why supercapacitors suit IoT and wearables
points: Useful for sensors that need quick bursts of power.
Supports short high-current events such as wireless transmission.
slides.say: Use smartwatch/sensor node examples.
slides.ask: Ask students to connect the construction to the direction of ion/electron movement.

slides.title: Ultra-small asymmetric supercapacitor
points: An asymmetric supercapacitor uses two different electrode materials so that the positive and negative electrodes store charge by different but complementary mechanisms.
slides.say: Explain asymmetric means electrode materials/functions are not identical.
slides.ask: Ask students to connect the construction to the direction of ion/electron movement.

slides.title: Construction of ultra-small asymmetric supercapacitor
points: It contains a positive electrode, negative electrode, ion-conducting electrolyte, separator/current collector and compact packaging for miniature devices.
slides.say: Point to electrolyte and separator as central layers.
slides.ask: Ask students to connect the construction to the direction of ion/electron movement.

slides.title: Working of asymmetric supercapacitor
slides.say: Explain it stores energy by charge separation and surface reactions.
slides.ask: Ask students to connect the construction to the direction of ion/electron movement.

slides.title: Applications in IoT and wearable devices
points: Short bursts for measurement and wireless data transfer.
Quick energy delivery for low-power electronics.
Compact energy buffer for tiny circuits.
Works with batteries or energy harvesters to handle peak loads.
slides.say: Tie to syllabus phrase IoT/wearable devices.

slides.title: What is a fuel cell?
points: A fuel cell converts the chemical energy of continuously supplied fuel and oxidant directly into electrical energy through electrochemical reactions.
slides.say: Say it behaves like a cell but reactants are supplied from outside.
slides.ask: Ask students to connect the construction to the direction of ion/electron movement.

slides.title: Fuel cell vs battery
points: Energy capacity tied to cell mass
slides.say: Ask students why a fuel cell can operate continuously.

slides.title: What is a solid-oxide fuel cell?
points: A solid-oxide fuel cell is a high-temperature fuel cell that uses a solid ceramic oxide electrolyte to conduct oxide ions.
slides.say: Use ceramic electrolyte as the key identifier.
slides.ask: Ask students to connect the construction to the direction of ion/electron movement.

slides.title: Construction of SOFC
points: SOFC construction includes a porous anode, dense solid oxide electrolyte, porous cathode, fuel supply, air/oxygen supply and external circuit.
slides.say: Point out solid electrolyte separates gases and conducts ions.

slides.title: Working principle of SOFC
points: Oxide ions move through ceramic electrolyte
Electricity, heat and products are formed
slides.say: Mention hydrogen or hydrocarbons may be used as fuel depending on design.

slides.title: SOFC applications
points: High-temperature exhaust can be useful heat.
Works naturally with hydrogen-based fuel supply.

slides.title: What is a solar photovoltaic cell?
points: A photovoltaic cell converts sunlight directly into electrical energy using the photovoltaic effect in a semiconductor junction.
slides.say: Tell students this is a direct light-to-electricity device.

slides.title: Construction of a PV cell
points: A PV cell contains a p-type and n-type semiconductor junction, front metal grid, back contact, anti-reflection coating and protective glass/encapsulation.
slides.say: Point to p-n junction as the active region.

slides.title: What is green hydrogen?
points: Green hydrogen is hydrogen produced using renewable energy or clean pathways so that carbon emissions are minimized during production.
slides.say: Explain hydrogen is an energy carrier, not a primary energy source.

slides.title: Photocatalytic water splitting
points: Photocatalytic water splitting uses light-activated TiO2 to generate electron-hole pairs that drive water oxidation and reduction to form oxygen and hydrogen.

slides.title: Advantages of TiO2 photocatalytic route
points: TiO2 is chemically stable under many conditions.

slides.title: Common mistakes in Module 3

definition.text: Using standard cell equations for concentration cells without setting E°cell = 0

points: Forgetting concentration ratio order in Nernst numericals
Mixing electron flow with ion flow in batteries
Writing supercapacitors as if they are ordinary batteries
Explaining PV cells without the p-n junction field
Calling all hydrogen green without checking production route
